title: JSON with jq
summary: Read, filter, and reshape JSON with jq, then get plain text out for Bash and pass Bash values in safely.
intro: APIs, config files and structured logs all speak JSON, and Bash has no JSON parser of its own. jq is the standard tool: a small language of filters that reads JSON, picks out values, and writes new JSON or plain text. This lesson works on the files in `jsonbox`: one user, a list of users, orders with their items, a health check, and an event log with one JSON object per line. When you call a real API with curl, jq is how your script reads the answer.

steps.title: Navigate JSON
steps.body:
A jq program is a filter: JSON goes in, and JSON comes out. The simplest filter, `.`, passes its input through, pretty-printed. `.name` picks a field, `.address.city` follows a path, `.[0]` picks an array's first item, and `.[]` produces every item, one after another. A missing field gives `null`, not an error.

```bash
jq '.address.city' <<< '{"name": "Ada", "address": {"city": "Lisbon"}}'
```

`|` passes each result to the next filter, the way a shell pipe does, and `-r` prints strings raw, without their JSON quotes, which is what a script wants. `A // B` gives B when A is `null` or `false`, so it's how you write a default. Inside a string, `\(...)` inserts a value. Put the whole filter in single quotes, so the shell leaves its `$`, `|` and quotes alone.

```bash
jq -r '.[] | "\(.name) is \(.age // "unknown")"' <<< '[{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, {"name": "Lin"}]'
```

examples.title: Fields
examples.prompt: Print the whole user in `user.json`, then its name as JSON and as plain text, its field names, and whether it has a phone.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq . user.json
jq .name user.json
jq -r .name user.json
jq -c 'keys' user.json
jq 'has("phone")' user.json
examples.output:
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Ada",
  "email": "ada@example.com",
  "role": "admin",
  "active": true,
  "address": {
    "street": "12 Rua das Flores",
    "city": "Lisbon",
    "country": "PT"
  },
  "tags": [
    "billing",
    "beta"
  ],
  "created_at": "2025-03-14T10:22:00Z"
}
"Ada"
Ada
["active","address","created_at","email","id","name","role","tags"]
false
examples.explanation: `.` prints the whole document with two-space indents. `.name` is a JSON string, so jq prints it with its quotes, and `-r` (raw) drops them, which is what you want in a variable or a loop. `keys` lists an object's field names in sorted order, and `-c` prints the result on one line. `has("phone")` asks whether a field exists, and this user has no phone.

examples.title: Arrays
examples.prompt: Pick from `users.json`, which is an array of users: the first user's email, every name, and how many users there are.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq '.[0].email' users.json
jq -r '.[].name' users.json
jq 'length' users.json
examples.output:
"ada.park@example.com"
Ada Park
Bruno Costa
Chioma Eze
Dmitri Volkov
Siobhan O'Brien
Elif Demir
Farid Haddad
Greta Lund
Hugo Martins
Ines Rocha
10
examples.explanation: `.[0]` is the first user, so `.[0].email` is that user's email. `.[]` produces each item in turn, and `.[].name` the name of each, one per line with `-r`. `length` counts the items of an array. On an object it counts the fields, and on a string the characters.

examples.title: Nested and missing
examples.prompt: Read a city two levels down, see what a missing one gives, supply a default, and build a sentence from one user.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq -r '.[0].address.city' users.json
jq '.[3].address.city' users.json
jq -r '.[3].address.city // "unknown"' users.json
jq -r '.[4] | "\(.name) lives in \(.address.city)"' users.json
examples.output:
Lisbon
null
unknown
Siobhan O'Brien lives in Dublin
examples.explanation: The user at index 3 (counting from 0) has no `address`, and jq doesn't fail on the missing path: `.address` is `null`, and `.city` of `null` is `null` too. `//` swaps in a default for `null`. The last command pipes one user into a string, where each `\(...)` inserts a value, so you build exactly the line you want. The name `Siobhan O'Brien` holds a quote, and it's no trouble here because it's data, not part of the filter.

steps.title: Filter and transform
steps.body:
`select(condition)` keeps an item when the condition is true and drops it otherwise, so `.[] | select(.active)` produces only the active users. Put a filter inside `[...]` to collect its results into an array. `map(f)` runs `f` on every item of an array and keeps the results as an array: `map(.total)` is the same as `[.[] | .total]`.

To build objects, `{name, email}` copies those two fields, and `{id, total: (.qty * .price)}` adds a computed one. Arrays have functions of their own: `length`, `add` (the sum), `sort_by(.field)`, `reverse`, `.[:3]` (the first three), `group_by(.field)`, `unique_by(.field)`, `min_by(.field)` and `max_by(.field)`.

```bash
jq -c 'map({sku, line: (.qty * .price)}) | max_by(.line)' <<< '[{"sku": "MUG", "qty": 3, "price": 9}, {"sku": "LAMP", "qty": 1, "price": 49}]'
```

examples.title: select
examples.prompt: Keep the users that match a condition: the active ones, the admins (counted), and the active editors.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq -r '.[] | select(.active) | .name' users.json
jq '[.[] | select(.role == "admin")] | length' users.json
jq -r '.[] | select(.role == "editor" and .active) | .email' users.json
examples.output:
Ada Park
Bruno Costa
Dmitri Volkov
Siobhan O'Brien
Elif Demir
Greta Lund
Hugo Martins
Ines Rocha
2
bruno.costa@example.com
dmitri.volkov@example.com
hugo.martins@example.com
examples.explanation: `select(.active)` keeps the users whose `active` is `true`. `select(.role == "admin")` compares a field, and wrapping the whole thing in `[...]` collects the matches into an array, so `length` can count them. Conditions combine with `and` and `or`, so the last line keeps editors who are also active.

examples.title: Reshape
examples.prompt: Build smaller objects: a user's contact card, the item count of the first orders, and each line total of one order.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq -c '{name, email, city: .address.city}' user.json
jq -c 'map({id, items: (.items | length)}) | .[:3]' orders.json
jq -c '.[2].items | map({name, line_total: (.qty * .price)})' orders.json
examples.explanation: `{name, email}` is short for `{name: .name, email: .email}`, and `city: .address.city` names a value from deeper in. `map` builds one object per order, with `(.items | length)` in parentheses as a value, and `.[:3]` keeps the first three. Arithmetic works on numbers, so each line total is `.qty * .price`.

examples.title: Sort and group
examples.prompt: Find the three biggest orders, count the orders in each status, and add up the pending totals.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq -c 'sort_by(.total) | reverse | .[:3] | map({id, total})' orders.json
jq -c 'group_by(.status) | map({status: .[0].status, count: length})' orders.json
jq '[.[] | select(.status == "pending") | .total] | add' orders.json
examples.explanation: `sort_by(.total)` sorts from low to high, `reverse` flips it, and `.[:3]` keeps three: the biggest orders. `group_by(.status)` sorts by status and splits the array into one array per status, so `.[0].status` names each group and `length` counts it. `add` sums an array of numbers, here the totals of the pending orders.

practice.title: Order summary
practice.starter:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# TODO: one compact {id, customer, total} line per paid order, highest total first
# TODO: then one {"paid":N,"revenue":X} line for the paid orders
jq -c '.[0] | {id, customer, total}' orders.json
practice.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

jq -c 'map(select(.status == "paid")) | sort_by(.total) | reverse | .[] | {id, customer, total}' orders.json
jq -c 'map(select(.status == "paid")) | {paid: length, revenue: (map(.total) | add)}' orders.json
hints: `map(select(.status == "paid"))` keeps just the paid orders, as an array.
For the order lines, continue with `sort_by(.total) | reverse | .[] | {id, customer, total}`, and run jq with `-c`.
Run a second `jq -c` that starts from the same paid array and builds `{paid: length, revenue: (map(.total) | add)}`.

steps.title: jq in scripts
steps.body:
In a script, jq sits between JSON and Bash, and both directions have a safe way.

Out of jq: `@tsv` and `@csv` turn an array into one line of tab or comma separated values, printed with `-r`. Names don't contain tabs, so `@tsv` pairs well with `while IFS=$'\t' read -r`.

Into jq: never paste a variable into the filter text, where a quote in the value breaks it. Pass the value with `--arg name value`, and the filter sees `$name` as a string. `--argjson` passes a number or other JSON instead, and `-n` runs a filter with no input, to build new JSON.

```bash
jq -n -c --arg user "O'Brien" --argjson age 36 '{user: $user, age: $age}'
```

`-e` sets jq's exit status from its last output, 1 for `false` or `null`, so `if jq -e ...` works. `-s` (slurp) reads every JSON value in the input into one array, which turns a file of JSON lines into something `length` and `map` can use. Since jq 1.7, `pick(.a.b)` keeps only the paths you name.

examples.title: Text for loops
examples.prompt: Print a table of users from a Bash loop fed by `@tsv`, then the first two users as CSV.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

while IFS=$'\t' read -r id name role; do
  printf '%-4s %-16s %s\n' "$id" "$name" "$role"
done < <(jq -r '.[] | [.id, .name, .role] | @tsv' users.json)

jq -r '.[:2][] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv' users.json
examples.output:
104  Ada Park         admin
101  Bruno Costa      editor
109  Chioma Eze       viewer
102  Dmitri Volkov    editor
107  Siobhan O'Brien  admin
103  Elif Demir       viewer
110  Farid Haddad     editor
105  Greta Lund       viewer
108  Hugo Martins     editor
106  Ines Rocha       viewer
104,"Ada Park","ada.park@example.com"
101,"Bruno Costa","bruno.costa@example.com"
examples.explanation: `[.id, .name, .role] | @tsv` turns each user into one tab separated line, and `IFS=$'\t'` makes `read` split on tabs only, so `Siobhan O'Brien`, with its space and its quote, stays one field. Feeding the loop with `< <(...)` keeps it in the main shell, as with any command. `@csv` writes the same kind of row as CSV: strings in double quotes, numbers bare, ready for a spreadsheet.

examples.title: Values in
examples.prompt: Build JSON from a title that contains double quotes, first by pasting it into the filter, then with `--arg`, and find a user by a name with a quote in it.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

title='Fix "login" bug'
jq -n "{title: \"$title\"}" 2> /dev/null || echo "pasted into the filter: jq can't parse it"
jq -n -c --arg title "$title" --argjson priority 2 '{title: $title, priority: $priority}'

name="Siobhan O'Brien"
jq -r --arg name "$name" '.[] | select(.name == $name) | .email' users.json
examples.explanation: Pasting `$title` into the filter text puts its quotes into jq's program, and jq stops with a syntax error (its message is hidden here). `--arg title "$title"` passes the value as data instead: inside the filter, `$title` is a string, and jq escapes its quotes when it writes JSON. `--argjson` passes JSON, so `priority` arrives as the number 2, not the string `"2"`. Filtering works the same way: `select(.name == $name)` finds the user whatever characters the name holds.

examples.title: Exit status and JSON lines
examples.prompt: Turn the health check's status into an `if`, then count the events in a JSON lines file by level.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if jq -e '.status == "ok"' health.json > /dev/null; then
  echo "healthy"
else
  echo "unhealthy: $(jq -r '.status' health.json)"
fi

jq -s 'map(select(.level == "error")) | length' events.jsonl
jq -s -r 'group_by(.level) | map("\(.[0].level): \(length)") | .[]' events.jsonl
examples.explanation: With `-e`, jq exits 1 when its last output is `false` or `null`, so the comparison drives `if` directly, and `> /dev/null` hides the `true` it prints. With a `health.json` whose status is `degraded`, the same script prints `unhealthy: degraded`. `events.jsonl` holds one JSON object per line, not an array, so `-s` slurps them all into one array first, and then `map`, `group_by` and `length` work on the whole file.

practice.title: Users to CSV
practice.prompt:
Export the users that have one role as CSV.

1. Print the header `id,name,email`.
2. Then print one `@csv` row per user whose `role` equals the `ROLE` environment variable, passed to jq with `--arg`, sorted by id.
3. When no user has that role, print only the header.

Test 1 runs with `ROLE=admin`.

Expected output:

```text
id,name,email
104,"Ada Park","ada.park@example.com"
107,"Siobhan O'Brien","siobhan.obrien@example.com"
```
practice.starter:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

role="${ROLE:?set ROLE to a role, like admin}"
echo "id,name,email"
# TODO: one @csv row per user whose role is $role (pass it with --arg), sorted by id
practice.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

role="${ROLE:?set ROLE to a role, like admin}"
echo "id,name,email"
jq -r --arg role "$role" 'map(select(.role == $role)) | sort_by(.id) | .[] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv' users.json

tests.output:
id,name,email
204,"Umar Farouk","umar.farouk@example.com"
207,"Sven Olsen","sven.olsen@example.com"
209,"Oliver Grant","oliver.grant@example.com"
210,"Quentin Moreau","quentin.moreau@example.com"
212,"Lina Haddad","lina.haddad@example.com"

hints: `jq -r --arg role "$role" '...'` makes `$role` a string inside the filter.
Keep the matching users with `map(select(.role == $role))`, then order them with `sort_by(.id)`.
Turn each user into a row with `.[] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv`.

recap:
- `.` pretty-prints, `.a.b` follows a path, `.[0]` picks an item, `.[]` produces every item, and `|` chains filters.
- `-r` prints raw strings for scripts, and `-c` prints each JSON value on one line.
- A missing field is `null`, and `A // B` supplies a default.
- `select(cond)` filters, `map(f)` transforms, `[...]` collects, and `{name, total: (.qty * .price)}` builds objects.
- `sort_by`, `reverse`, `.[:3]`, `group_by`, `unique_by`, `min_by`, `max_by`, `length` and `add` work on arrays.
- `"\(.name) <\(.email)>"` builds text, and `@tsv` or `@csv` builds lines for Bash.
- Pass values in with `--arg` for strings or `--argjson` for JSON, never by pasting them into the filter.
- `-e` turns a result into an exit status, and `-s` slurps JSON lines into one array.
